extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and methodology (advanced undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the nature, origin, and certainty of axioms, definitions, and demonstrations in deductive (mathematical/logical) and inductive sciences; contrasts supposed a priori necessity with experimental/hypothetical origins. Useful for philosophers, methodologists, and scientists reflecting on justification of principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms are inductions from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms are but a class, the most universal class, of inductions from experience; the simplest and easiest cases of generalization from the facts furnished to us by our senses or by our internal consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the evidential status of axioms should be treated as empirical — they rest on superabundant and obvious evidence. Burden of proof lies on those who claim any other origin (i.e., a priori or non-experimental). Example discussion: laws of motion and chemical laws were historically collected from experience and later felt as 'self-evident' only after long habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are generalizations, not exact truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (as commonly called in demonstrative sciences) are generalizations from experience which are not even, accurately speaking, truths; being propositions in which, while we assert of some kind of object some property which observation shows to belong to it, we at the same time deny that it possesses any other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: treat many 'definitions' as convenient fictions that exclude modifying circumstances to simplify reasoning. When evaluating a demonstrative argument, check which modifying circumstances have been excluded and whether exclusion is justified for the case at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive sciences are hypothetical and conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive or Demonstrative Sciences are all, without exception, Inductive Sciences; they are also, in virtue of the peculiar character of one indispensable portion of the general formulæ according to which their inductions are made, Hypothetical Sciences. Their conclusions are only true on certain suppositions, which are, or ought to be, approximations to the truth, but are seldom, if ever, exactly true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging deductions, separate two tasks: (a) trace consequences of assumptions (demonstrative part), (b) separately assess whether assumptions are true or close enough to truth (empirical part). Do not conflate logical validity with empirical adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of a priori necessity require proof beyond habit
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance that some truths are 'necessary' or 'self-evident' often results from habitual association and the progressive formation of a scientific cast of mind; such apparent inconceivableness is accidental and dependent on mental history, not an intrinsic property of the proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate assertions that something is 'inconceivable' or 'necessarily true' by examining historical contingency and whether familiarity, training, or repeated confirmation produced the impression of necessity. Examples: resistance to heliocentrism, acceptance of Newtonian refrangibility, belief in definite chemical proportions after experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical propositions are not merely verbal conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that propositions of the science of numbers are merely verbal (definitions) and that arithmetic/algebra is only substitution of expressions is inadequate: there is in every step of an arithmetical or algebraical calculation a real induction, a real inference of facts from facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing mathematical reasoning, recognize the underlying inductive grounding: numbers are always 'numbers of something' and arithmetical truths apply to all things by induction. Beware of reducing arithmetic to mere synonymy of terms; trace the induction that justifies numeric claims (e.g., demonstrating 'three is two and one' depends on observable aggregations of objects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty is limited to pure number
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty... is not an attribute of all mathematical truths, but of those only which relate to pure Number, as distinguished from Quantity in the more enlarged sense; and only so long as we abstain from supposing that the numbers are a precise index to actual quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test claimed 'mathematical certainty' by checking whether the claim concerns pure number (abstract counting) or measured quantities (weights, lengths). If units or heterogeneous units are involved (troy vs avoirdupois, different standards), the certainty becomes hypothetical and contingent on empirical equivalence of units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic axioms rest on an implicit hypothesis of equal units
rubrics_metrics.description: All propositions concerning numbers imply the condition that 1=1; that all the numbers are numbers of the same or of equal units. Let this be doubtful, and not one of the propositions of arithmetic will hold true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying arithmetic to real-world quantities, explicitly verify the assumption of unit-homogeneity. Examples: adding pounds of different standards, comparing 'horsepower' unless horses are assumed equally strong. Failure to check units turns arithmetic into a mistaken application of pure-number results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions in geometry assert existence (not mere meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: We may call the proposition 'A circle is a figure bounded by a line ...' the definition of a circle; but the proposition from which so many consequences follow, and which is really a first principle in geometry, is, that figures answering to this description exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate geometric (or other definitional) systems by checking that their 'definitions' presuppose existence claims; ensure the existence of the defined kinds in the subject-matter before treating subsequent deductions as about real phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic manipulation conceals but does not eliminate induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Although algebraic symbols may be used without exciting ideas of particular things, the inferences drawn are concerning things, not mere signs; the probative force of the process is derived from induction applied to the magnitudes the symbols represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing symbolic proofs, ask what empirical or conceptual induction justifies treating the symbols as representatives of all relevant things. Do not accept purely formal manipulations as sufficient explanation of why the result applies to real-world cases unless the inductive link is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: The methodological separation of inference and empirical verification
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of course quite as practicable to arrive at new conclusions from facts assumed, as from facts observed... They proceed by tracing the consequences of certain assumptions; leaving for separate consideration whether the assumptions are true or not, and if not exactly true, whether they are a sufficiently near approximation to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rubric for evaluating scientific arguments, require explicit separation: (1) clearly state assumptions/hypotheses, (2) trace logical consequences, (3) independently evaluate empirical support for the assumptions and their adequacy. Score higher where authors make these separations explicit and analyze approximation errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake provisional hypothesis for self-evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis chosen for experimental inquiry will naturally be one which groups together some considerable number of facts already known. That the theory itself preceded the proof of its truth—that it had to be conceived before it could be proved, and in order that it might be proved—does not imply that it was self-evident, and did not need proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In peer review or critique, penalize arguments that treat a hypothesized framework as self-evident merely because it was useful to organize experiments. Require demonstration, not rhetorical appeal to obviousness. Examples: assuming conservation of mass provisionally for chemical analysis does not make it self-evident without experimental confirmation.
